video_title: Lawfare Daily: Censorship Incentives with Julia Curlee and Mike Feinberg
gist: Two purged national-security officials (ex-CIA/NSC and ex-FBI) describe a bureaucracy-wide, self-reinforcing incentive structure -- weaponized security clearances, a captured private-sector and think-tank job market, and Schedule F-style political control -- that keeps almost every other purged official from speaking publicly, and outline the small number of counter-incentive programs (like Lawfare's Public Service Fellowship) trying to break it.

insights.claim: Among CIA, DNI and DIA personnel who left involuntarily or under duress in the second Trump administration, Julia Curlee says she is, as far as she knows, the only one who has both landed outside government and spoken publicly about her experience.
insights.speaker: Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: Public whistleblowing from purged IC officials is essentially a sample size of one, meaning outside observers (investors, journalists, oversight bodies) are getting almost no independent visibility into what's happening inside the intelligence community.
insights.quote: of the people who have left in the second Trump administration, it's me.

insights.claim: In the FBI, Mike Feinberg counts only about four people (excluding himself) who have spoken publicly and specifically about their own situation, out of what he estimates are dozens to hundreds of agents who were fired, pushed to resign, or left prematurely because of the environment.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: A very small public-disclosure rate relative to the affected population suggests systemic chilling rather than isolated retaliation, which matters for assessing legal/reputational tail risk facing agencies and any firms that employ these alumni.
insights.quote: I can think of offhand four, not including myself

insights.claim: Two overlapping public disclosure efforts -- a New York Times narrative history piece and a Justice Connection video announcement -- share at least 75% of the same individuals, indicating the pool of FBI alumni willing to go public is even smaller than the number of media appearances suggests.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: Media coverage of dissenting former officials overstates the true breadth of willing whistleblowers, which analysts should discount when gauging how much institutional pushback is actually occurring.
insights.quote: those last two groups probably share 75, if not more, percent of the same membership

insights.claim: Mike Feinberg says he has been contacted by at least a hundred people still inside government who each say some version of 'I wish I could speak but I can't because of kids, mortgage, house, job.'
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: A three-digit count of self-identified silenced insiders reaching out to just one public figure implies the true base of chilled dissent across the federal workforce is large and systemic, not anecdotal.
insights.quote: it's got to be at least a hundred of people who send me an individual message that says, Thank you so much for speaking. I wish I could.

themes.theme: Security clearances and personnel process as political weapons

insights.claim: On day one of the second Trump administration, dozens of security clearances were revoked by executive order and announced via tweet with no review process and no appeal mechanism, reaching back nearly a decade to alleged offenses tied to the 2016 or 2020 elections.
insights.speaker: Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: A demonstrated willingness to strip livelihoods via unreviewable executive action, on day one, sets a low-cost precedent for using clearance revocation as a political weapon against any employee or contractor class going forward.
insights.quote: No review, no process. It clearly came in with a list of names that they were going to go after.

insights.claim: The FBI leadership began, even in the late Biden administration, taking a 'second bite at the apple': after an internal OPR (Office of Professional Responsibility) investigation concluded with a lighter-than-desired penalty, the security division would separately review whether the person should keep their clearance, effectively creating double jeopardy.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: A process precedent created under one administration became a ready-made lever for a more politically motivated administration to purge personnel without new legal authority -- a pattern worth watching wherever agencies build discretionary secondary-review mechanisms.
insights.quote: I think this was really shortsighted by bureau leadership because it was the very sort of thing that a less principled administration could leverage to its advantage going forward.

insights.claim: The security clearance system is a uniquely useful purge tool for the FBI specifically because, unlike other IC agencies, the FBI still has to justify personnel actions in ways that touch the public record; a clearance revocation avoids exposing classified case work while still ending a career.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: This is a generalizable mechanism: any agency wanting to remove personnel for political reasons without exposing itself to legal or public scrutiny can route the action through clearance/classification review rather than a public disciplinary process.
insights.quote: If you're going to get rid of them and you want to do it in a way that sends a message, it has to be based on something that does not implicate their still secret work.

insights.claim: The Director of National Intelligence intervened directly in CIA personnel decisions -- including officers rotated to the National Intelligence Council and analysts who had worked on the 2016 Russia assessment years earlier -- without any adjudication process, and CIA leadership did not resist this outside interference.
insights.speaker: Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: Cross-agency reach by a politically appointed DNI into another agency's personnel matters, unopposed by that agency's own leadership, signals an erosion of institutional independence investors should weight when assessing IC-adjacent contractors' operating stability.
insights.quote: the CIA leadership itself not standing up to block the DNI from interfering in from a CIA's perspective in basic personnel uh decisions in the agency

insights.claim: Publicly walking out well-regarded, widely-known CIA officers in front of the rest of the workforce functioned as a deliberate signal that no one was safe and that agency leadership would not intervene to protect anyone.
insights.speaker: Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: Visible, public retribution against high-status insiders is a far more efficient chilling mechanism than private discipline, because it maximizes deterrence per incident -- a pattern that predicts continued low internal dissent even absent further firings.
insights.quote: you really sent a chilling message through the workforce that no one was safe and the leadership of the organization would do nothing to help you.

insights.claim: Schedule F-style conversion of civil-service positions to at-will, politically evaluated roles is spreading beyond the White House into agencies like DoD (not yet CIA as of this taping), pushing political loyalty tests down to below the GS-15 level.
insights.speaker: Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: If political-loyalty evaluation criteria penetrate mid-level technical and analytic roles across the federal workforce, expect further degradation of independent expert judgment in procurement, regulatory, and intelligence functions relevant to government contractors and regulated industries.
insights.quote: It is now penetrating much deeper into the workforce which again adds to that censorship of people not willing to talk.

insights.claim: Historically, cabinet officials and agency heads were 'dual hatted' -- loyal to the president but also self-interestedly protective of their own agency's personnel and turf, because a protected workforce made the leader look effective; Mike Feinberg argues that dynamic is now gone for the first time in modern US history.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: This is a structural, not incident-specific, claim: if agency leadership no longer has self-interested reasons to shield staff, expect fewer internal checks on politically motivated personnel actions across the executive branch going forward, not just in this administration's IC purges.
insights.quote: The current leadership of the IC does not care one wit what the workforce thinks of them. And as a result, they're solely looking out for the administration at large.

insights.claim: The public appeals process for federal employees has been overwhelmed by tens of thousands of appeals filed into offices that have themselves been cut ('DOGE'd'), leaving little practical recourse, and probationary employees have even fewer avenues for appeal.
insights.speaker: Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: A deliberately or incidentally under-resourced appeals system functions as an additional silencing mechanism by making legal recourse practically unavailable, which matters for assessing wrongful-termination litigation risk and timelines against federal agencies.
insights.quote: the overwhelming of what few appeal places that there are for federal employees with tens of thousands of of of people appealing in offices that have themselves been doed and really no recourse uh being allowed to them.

themes.theme: The private-sector revolving door as a silencing mechanism

insights.claim: Feinberg describes three post-FBI career paths for special agents: outright retirement on pension, worker-level security/investigative consulting or work at another federal agency ('double dipping'), and senior-executive-level C-suite security roles at companies (often Fortune 500) that do business with government -- and it is this third group, with the most to say, that faces the strongest muzzling.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: The people best positioned to expose misconduct (senior former officials with institutional knowledge) are structurally the most economically captured, meaning public disclosure quality is inversely correlated with insider knowledge quality -- a durable information-asymmetry problem for oversight and markets alike.
insights.quote: the overwhelming majority of the senior executives who have been ousted from the FBI over the past year and a half, two years are in that position

insights.claim: Companies that hire former senior FBI/IC officials as security executives are 'incredibly loathed' to let them speak publicly because those companies do business with the government and don't want to jeopardize that relationship, particularly under an administration described as 'petty and vindictive.'
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: Corporate government-contracting relationships create a direct commercial incentive to suppress employee political speech, effectively privatizing censorship enforcement without any government action being formally required.
insights.quote: they are incredibly loathed to have any of their employees say anything that may get in the way of that relationship

insights.claim: Compensation in these roles ($400,000-$500,000/year range cited) functions as golden handcuffs that make the trade-off between speaking out and comfort a binary, high-stakes decision for senior alumni.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: Quantifies the private economic cost of speaking out for this population, useful for modeling how much a counter-incentive program (fellowship, alliance) would need to offset to change behavior at scale.
insights.quote: You're getting $400, $500,000 a year maybe

insights.claim: Even after retirement without being individually targeted, many alumni lack media training and public-writing experience, so they would not know how to speak effectively even if permitted to.
insights.speaker: Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: The silencing problem is not purely an incentive problem but also a capability gap -- meaning programs aimed at enabling speech need to provide media/communications training, not just financial runway.
insights.quote: they've never gotten media training. They've never interacted with the press. They haven't done any sort of public writing.

insights.claim: Julia Curlee, a former senior director for intelligence programs at the NSC, applied to over 100 jobs across nine months and did not get a single interview, which she attributes to being both a publicly purged official and a transgender person amid simultaneous DEI program rollbacks at prospective employers.
insights.speaker: Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: A concrete, extreme data point (0-for-100+) on the real-world employability cost of being publicly associated with a politically targeted purge -- relevant for valuing 'reputational contamination' risk that private-sector employers appear to price in.
insights.quote: in nine months of applying for probably over a hundred jobs, I did not get a single interview. Not one.

insights.claim: One article Mike Feinberg published about his resignation (five pages) was, in his assessment, enough to permanently preclude him from ever getting a private-sector security consulting job, and he frames corporate reluctance to hire outspoken alumni not as prudent risk aversion but as 'cowardice.'
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: A sharply against-consensus reframing that corporate risk-aversion around hiring outspoken former officials is a moral failure rather than neutral business prudence -- useful framing for ESG/governance analysts assessing corporate complicity in institutional erosion.
insights.quote: There is not a single Fortune 500 company whose prosperity has not been made possible except for the rule of law in this country and the free market and discourse of ideas that we have. To now turn a blind eye to the shifts that are undermining that environment is fundamentally to pull up the bridge behind you.

themes.theme: Think tanks and civil society: funding fragility as leverage

insights.claim: Julia Curlee found DC-area think tanks to be even more risk-averse than private companies because their operating budgets are razor-thin and often depend on federal grants or seconded/paid federal fellowship positions, making them vulnerable to funders pulling support.
insights.speaker: Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: Nonprofit/think-tank funding structure is a specific, exploitable point of leverage over public discourse; investors or philanthropists interested in supporting independent policy voices should note that federal-grant dependence is a direct vulnerability.
insights.quote: perhaps they were even more riskaverse than than private companies because of how razor thin their operating budgets are

insights.claim: The administration directed the IRS early on to investigate whether tax-exempt entities were financing disfavored kinds of speech; Curlee says little of this materialized in practice but it still deterred donors, who in turn eliminated fellowships and shut off speaking opportunities.
insights.speaker: Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: Regulatory threat alone -- without enforcement actually materializing -- can achieve a chilling effect via donor deterrence, illustrating that legal risk to nonprofit funders doesn't need to be realized to be effective as censorship.
insights.quote: that had a chilling effect... it did deter the donors who then deter the then prevent the the fellowships

insights.claim: The Stanford Internet Observatory was 'destroyed' by a combination of state attorneys general investigations and congressional investigations built on a theory pressed against the entity and its individuals (Renée DiResta named as one of its principals) -- cited as a concrete precedent showing think tanks' risk fears are well-founded, not paranoid.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: A named, verifiable case study of a research institution being effectively dismantled via legal/political pressure over content-moderation-adjacent research -- a template pattern investors in media/trust-and-safety/research organizations should track as replicable risk.
insights.quote: that was destroyed by a series of state AGs and and uh congressional investigations that concocted a theory about them

insights.claim: A third exit path for purged officials -- joining civil-society/advocacy organizations that litigate against administration policy (e.g., the path taken by whistleblower attorney figures and some Jack Smith prosecutors) -- has only absorbed a small number of people and is limited by the same funding fragility affecting think tanks.
insights.speaker: Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: The 'go work for the resistance' pathway often assumed to be an easy safety valve for purged officials is in fact capacity-constrained, meaning it cannot scale to absorb the volume of silenced alumni the guests describe.
insights.quote: A lot of it is the funding base.

themes.theme: Congress as an under-recognized threat vector

insights.claim: Mike Feinberg argues Congress poses a greater independent danger to research organizations than the FBI does, because the FBI is ultimately answerable to courts and risks becoming 'a laughingstock' if it overreaches, whereas members like Jim Jordan can issue subpoenas without facing equivalent accountability.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: A counterintuitive risk-ranking useful for legal/compliance risk modeling: congressional investigative power, not just executive-branch law enforcement, is flagged as the more potent and less checked threat to institutions engaged in politically sensitive research.
insights.quote: it's not necessarily the FBI, right? ... they do ultimately have to produce the goods ... whereas when Jim Jordan does the equivalent thing he doesn't make himself a laughingstock actually he just gets to throw out subpoenas

themes.theme: Counter-incentive structures and the reward side of compliance

insights.claim: The Lawfare Public Service Fellowship is designed as a deliberate counter-incentive structure -- providing salary, a publishing outlet, and a track record -- modeled on how intelligence agencies historically built career incentives (promotion for speaking up) to make dissent survivable rather than requiring individual heroism.
insights.speaker: Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: A generalizable institutional-design template: pairing bridge income with a publication platform is presented as the mechanism that actually offsets the private-sector/think-tank silencing incentive described elsewhere in the episode.
insights.quote: it's a very unique entity as far as I can tell in the broader uh media and and and uh think tank world.

insights.claim: Besides Lawfare's fellowship, only a few comparable counter-incentive programs exist: a Democracy Forward effort hiring people to document administration-era damage and chart a path for the next administration, and the Public Service Alliance, a new organization (stood up within the last roughly three years, specifically in response to this environment) offering discounted services including defense against online harassment campaigns for former federal employees.
insights.speaker: Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: Names a small, specific set of investable/fundable organizations addressing this gap -- useful map for philanthropic or impact-oriented capital looking to support institutional-accountability infrastructure.
insights.quote: the public service alliance, it's worth noting, is an organization that was stood up entirely in response to the current situation.

insights.claim: Curlee alleges that on the reward side, businesses encouraging investors to make investments benefiting the president's family have been rewarded with government contracts, and she expects future investigations to find that prominent DC consulting and advisory firms gave advice bordering on unethical in order to personally enrich members of the president's family.
insights.speaker: Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: A forward-looking legal/reputational tail-risk flag for DC-area consulting and advisory firms: the guest predicts future investigations into pay-to-play dynamics tied to contracts and family-adjacent investments, which is a scenario worth monitoring for firms in that space.
insights.quote: I don't doubt that investigations will find that prominent DC firms and consulting businesses have been giving people advice that borders on certainly the unethical

insights.claim: Feinberg frames the current situation as 'backsliding' toward authoritarianism rather than full authoritarianism, but notes that for discrete populations in specific enforcement operations (he names Minneapolis during 'Metro Surge' and Chicago during 'Midway Blitz') conditions may already feel authoritarian.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: Distinguishes uneven, population-specific severity of state action from a uniform national narrative -- relevant for assessing localized operational, legal, and reputational risk tied to specific federal enforcement surges rather than assuming uniform national conditions.
insights.quote: There are places like Minneapolis during Metro Surge or Chicago during Midway Blitz where it may very much feel like that and in fact be that for discreet populations. But that doesn't mean we're not backsliding either.
